analysis.one_liner: Expands health coverage to millions by banning preexisting-condition denials and subsidizing insurance for low- and middle-income families.
analysis.headline: The Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act became Public Law 111-148 on March 23, 2010, after the Senate passed it 60-39 and the House passed the final version 219-212.
analysis.plain_summary: This law requires health insurers to sell to everyone regardless of health status, bans lifetime and annual dollar limits on coverage, and stops insurers from canceling policies after someone gets sick. It creates a marketplace where households earning between 100% and 400% of the poverty line get refundable tax credits for premiums, and expands Medicaid to cover adults up to 133% of poverty, with the federal government paying the full cost of the new expansion population from 2014 to 2016. Children can stay on a parent's plan until age 26, and most plans must cover preventive services without cost-sharing. The bill also imposes new requirements on hospitals, drug makers, insurers, and large employers, and new fees on insurers, drug makers, and high-income households.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured Americans, people with preexisting conditions who were previously denied or priced out of coverage, low- and middle-income households earning 100-400% of poverty who get premium tax credits, young adults covered to age 26 on their parents' plans, low-income families gaining Medicaid, and small businesses claiming a tax credit for employee coverage.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured and low- and middle-income families

how_it_helps.text: Bars insurers from denying coverage or setting waiting periods based on preexisting conditions, and prohibits annual or lifetime dollar limits on essential benefits, so a serious illness can no longer exhaust someone's policy.
Prohibits insurers from rescinding (canceling) an enrollee's policy except for fraud or intentional misrepresentation, ending the practice of canceling coverage after a costly diagnosis.
Provides refundable tax credits for premiums and reduced out-of-pocket cost-sharing for households earning between 100% and 400% of the federal poverty line.
Extends Medicaid, starting in 2014, to adults under 65 with incomes at or below 133% of poverty, with the federal government paying 100% of the cost of newly eligible people through 2016.
Requires plans to allow children to stay on a parent's coverage until age 26, and to cover recommended preventive services with no cost-sharing for the enrollee.

Requires insurers to spend at least 85% (large-group) or 80% (individual and small-group) of premium dollars on medical care or quality improvement, and rebate the difference to enrollees; requires public hospital charge lists and standardized, plain-language coverage summaries.
Gives small employers with up to 25 employees earning under $50,000 on average a tax credit for 50% of employee health coverage expenses.
Requires drug makers to provide bigger Medicaid rebates and to discount brand-name drugs for seniors who fall into the Medicare Part D coverage gap.

analysis.who_pays: Large employers who do not offer qualifying coverage to full-time workers face fines; health insurers, brand-name drug makers, and medical device makers pay new annual fees; taxpayers earning over $200,000 ($250,000 per couple) pay a 0.9% additional Medicare tax; high-cost employer health plans face a 40% excise tax above set thresholds; and consumers buy indoor tanning services pay a new 10% tax.
analysis.who_pays_short: Insurers, drug and device makers, high earners, large employers

drawbacks.text: Requires most individuals to maintain minimum essential coverage or pay a penalty starting in 2014, with exemptions for low-income people who cannot afford coverage, hardship, religious objections, and others.

Fines large employers (more than 50 full-time employees) that fail to offer minimum essential coverage or that impose long enrollment waiting periods, and requires employers with over 200 employees to automatically enroll new hires.

Imposes a 40% excise tax on the value of high-cost employer-sponsored health coverage above $8,500 for individual and $23,000 for family plans (higher for retirees and high-risk professions such as law enforcement and emergency responders).

Imposes a 0.9% additional Medicare payroll tax on earnings over $200,000 per individual or $250,000 per couple, and new annual fees on health insurers, branded drug makers, and medical device manufacturers, which supporters acknowledged could be passed to consumers through premiums.
Bars generic competition for biosimilar biological drugs for 12 years after the brand-name product is licensed, a provision criticized for delaying cheaper alternatives.
Prohibits federal funds from being used for abortion services and requires separate accounts for abortion coverage, and lets states prohibit abortion coverage in plans sold on the exchanges.

Includes a Nebraska-specific provision that after 2017 requires the federal government to pay 100% of the cost of Medicaid expansion in that state alone, a carve-out widely criticized as favoring one state.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core achievement is structural: insurers can no longer deny, cancel, or cap coverage based on health, and tens of millions of uninsured Americans gained subsidized coverage through expanded Medicaid and tax credits. The costs are real but concentrated and deliberate — penalties on large employers, fees on insurers and drug makers, a surtax on households earning over $200,000, and an excise tax on the most generous employer plans. The mandate that individuals buy coverage drew the most sustained criticism, since it directs people to purchase from private companies; the 12-year biosimilar exclusivity and the Nebraska-specific federal funding carve-out were the most obvious concessions to narrow interests inside an otherwise consumer-directed bill. On balance, the direct benefits to working families outweigh the drawbacks, though some of the financing will reach consumers through premiums.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed an unrelated tax bill, the Senate rewrote it into the health care overhaul, the House then accepted the Senate's version unchanged, and the President signed it into law on March 23, 2010.

narrative.text: Introduced on September 17, 2009 as the Service Members Home Ownership Tax Act of 2009 — a bill extending the first-time homebuyer tax credit for military service members and raising corporate estimated tax payments — it was referred to the Ways and Means Committee.
The House passed the bill as a tax measure on October 8, 2009, by 416-0 with no member of either party opposed, under a fast-track procedure requiring a two-thirds majority.

The Senate used the bill as the vehicle for health care reform, and on November 21, 2009 invoked cloture on a motion to proceed by exactly 60-39, with all 58 voting Democrats, one independent Democrat, and one independent in favor and all 39 Republicans opposed.

Senate Republicans repeatedly moved to commit (send) the bill to the Finance Committee with instructions — by Senators McCain, Hatch, Johanns, Crapo, and Hutchison — to stall debate; every motion failed by votes of 42-58, 41-57, 41-53, 42-57, and 45-54, and a Hutchison motion was tabled 56-41.

After weeks of Senate debate, cloture was invoked 60-39 on December 23, and the Senate passed the amended bill by 60-39 on December 24, 2009, again with every voting Democrat and both independents in favor and every Republican opposed.
On March 21, 2010, the House agreed to the Senate amendments by 219-212: all 219 voting Democrats in favor, 34 Democrats opposed, and all 178 voting Republicans opposed.
The President signed the bill on March 23, 2010, and it became Public Law 111-148, the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The uninsured and lower-income households gained guaranteed coverage, no preexisting-condition denials, and premium subsidies; health insurers also gained a pool of millions of new subsidized customers, though they accepted new coverage rules and fees. The law's opponents won structural victories inside the bill — no public option, the individual mandate instead, 12-year biosimilar exclusivity, and the abortion-funding restrictions.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The uninsured, who gained guaranteed coverage

for.name: President Barack Obama
for.what_they_did: Signed the bill on March 23, 2010, making it Public Law 111-148.

for.name: Rep. Charles B. Rangel
for.role: House sponsor, Ways and Means Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the House on September 17, 2009.

for.name: Sen. Harry Reid
for.what_they_did: Managed the Senate debate, filed the cloture motions that kept the bill moving, and used it as the vehicle for the health care overhaul.

for.name: Rep. Earl Blumenauer
for.role: House floor manager for the original tax bill
for.what_they_did: Moved to suspend the rules and pass the bill, sending it to the Senate as the vehicle for reform.

for.name: 58 Democratic senators and both independents
for.what_they_did: Provided exactly the 60 votes needed to overcome three attempted filibusters on motions and on final passage, 60-39 each time.

against.name: 178 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Cast all 178 Republican votes against final passage on March 21, 2010, which nearly defeated the bill at 219-212.

against.name: 39 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted unanimously against the motion to proceed, cloture on the bill, and final passage; because 60 votes were required to end debate, their unified opposition made every vote razor-thin.

against.name: Sens. John McCain, Orrin Hatch, Mike Johanns, Mike Crapo, and Kay Bailey Hutchison
against.what_they_did: Repeatedly moved to send the bill back to committee with instructions to slow or kill debate; every motion was rejected, and final floor votes defeated them 42-58, 41-57, 41-53, 42-57, 45-54, and 56-41.

against.name: 34 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted against final House passage of the Senate-amended bill, the only members of the majority to defect.

sides.party_line_note: The fight ran almost entirely along party lines: the final House vote was 219-212 with every voting Republican opposed and 34 Democrats joining them, and every Senate vote on proceeding, cloture, and passage fell 60-39 or 45-54 with zero Republicans in favor.
